question_text: The cloud type usually associated with steady rain is

choices.text: altostratus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: altocumulus.

choices.label: C
choices.text: stratocumulus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: nimbostratus.

explanation: Nimbostratus is a thick, layered cloud that typically produces continuous, steady precipitation over a wide area.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Altocumulus is a mid-level cloud not typically associated with steady rain.

learning_objective: Explain why cloud forms when moist warm air overruns cold air.
question_text: Clouds form when moist warm air overruns cold air because the warm air

choices.label: A
choices.text: is cooled by the cold air underneath.

choices.label: B
choices.text: is cooled by the surrounding cold air aloft.

choices.label: C
choices.text: becomes unstable as a result of cooling from below.

choices.label: D
choices.text: cools as a result of expansion as it rises.

explanation: As warm air is forced to rise over the retreating cold air mass (overrunning), it expands and cools adiabatically with altitude; once cooled to its dew point, cloud forms.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Direct conductive cooling from the cold air underneath is not the primary mechanism; adiabatic expansion cooling as the air rises is.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The warm air is above, not surrounded by, the cold air aloft in this scenario; the cooling mechanism is expansion from lifting.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Overrunning warm air is being lifted and is typically stable relative to the frontal surface, not made unstable by cooling from below.

choices.label: C
choices.text: moist air is influenced by orographic effect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: moist cool air moves from a cold surface to a warm surface.

explanation: Advection fog forms when moist air is carried horizontally (advected) from a relatively warm surface to a colder surface, where it is cooled below its dew point.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: That mechanism describes radiation fog, not advection fog.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: That describes upslope/orographic fog, a different fog type.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This reverses the correct direction: advection fog forms moving from warm to cold, not cold to warm.

question_text: Radiation fog forms as a result of the

choices.label: A
choices.text: passage of cold air over a warm surface.

choices.label: B
choices.text: air becoming moist as it moves over the sea.

choices.label: C
choices.text: clouds becoming cold and heavy at night so that they settle to the ground.

choices.label: D
choices.text: ground becoming cold at night and cooling the air in contact with it.

explanation: Radiation fog forms when the ground radiates heat away and cools rapidly, typically on clear, calm nights, cooling the air layer in contact with it below its dew point.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Cold air over a warm surface describes a different (advective/stability) scenario, not the radiational cooling mechanism.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Moistening over the sea describes a moisture-source process, not the radiative cooling that defines this fog type.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Clouds do not physically 'settle to the ground' to form fog; radiation fog forms in place from surface-layer cooling.

learning_objective: State the wind circulation direction around high and low pressure areas in the northern hemisphere.
question_text: In the northern hemisphere, the winds blow

choices.label: A
choices.text: clockwise around high and low pressure areas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: counter-clockwise around high and low pressure areas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: clockwise around a high pressure area and counter-clockwise around a low pressure area.

choices.label: D
choices.text: counter-clockwise around a high pressure area and clockwise around a low pressure area.

explanation: In the northern hemisphere, the Coriolis effect causes winds to circulate clockwise around high-pressure areas (anticyclonic) and counter-clockwise around low-pressure areas (cyclonic).

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The rotation direction differs between highs and lows; it is not the same (clockwise) for both.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This reverses both rotation directions from the correct northern-hemisphere pattern.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This reverses the correct pairing: highs are clockwise, lows are counter-clockwise, not the other way around.

learning_objective: Describe how wind typically changes during a descent from 2,000 feet AGL to the surface.
question_text: During a descent from 2,000 feet AGL to the surface, you will usually find that the wind

choices.label: A
choices.text: veers and increases.

choices.label: B
choices.text: backs and increases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: veers and decreases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: backs and decreases.

explanation: Surface friction slows and backs the wind relative to the gradient wind aloft, so descending toward the surface, wind speed typically decreases and wind direction backs (shifts counter-clockwise) compared to its value at 2,000 feet AGL.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Wind veers and speeds up with increasing height (moving away from the surface), not on descent toward it.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Wind backs on descent, but speed decreases (due to friction), not increases.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Wind decreases in speed on descent, but it backs, not veers.

learning_objective: Describe the diurnal (day/night) change in surface wind velocity.
question_text: The diurnal change of surface wind velocity is such that during the day the surface wind will usually

choices.label: A
choices.text: veer and increase in speed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: veer and decrease in speed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: back and increase in speed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: back and decrease in speed.

explanation: Daytime solar heating drives convective mixing that brings faster, more veered wind from aloft down to the surface, so daytime surface wind typically veers and increases in speed compared to its nighttime values.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Daytime wind speed increases, not decreases, due to convective mixing.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Daytime wind veers, not backs, as mixing brings the gradient wind's direction closer to the surface.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Both the direction and speed change described here are opposite the typical daytime pattern.

learning_objective: Calculate the standard-atmosphere temperature at 5,000 feet.
question_text: In the standard atmosphere, the temperature at an altitude of 5,000 feet will be closest to

choices.label: A
choices.text: 0ºC.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5ºC.

choices.label: C
choices.text: 8ºC.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 10ºC.

explanation: The International Standard Atmosphere defines a sea-level temperature of 15°C with a lapse rate of approximately 2°C per 1,000 ft; at 5,000 ft this gives 15 - (2 x 5) = 5°C.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 0°C corresponds to roughly 7,500 ft in the standard atmosphere, not 5,000 ft.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 8°C does not match the standard 2°C/1,000 ft lapse-rate calculation for 5,000 ft.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 10°C corresponds to roughly 2,500 ft, not 5,000 ft, in the standard atmosphere.

regulation_reference: ICAO Standard Atmosphere definition, as taught in Canadian PPL/RPP groundschool.
calculation_steps: Standard sea-level temperature = 15°C. Standard lapse rate ≈ 2°C per 1,000 ft. Temperature at 5,000 ft = 15 - (2 x 5) = 5°C.

learning_objective: List the conditions required for thunderstorm formation.
question_text: The conditions required for the formation of thunderstorms are

choices.label: A
choices.text: moist air, high temperature, and an inversion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: stratus cloud, high humidity and a lifting force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: unstable air, high humidity and a lifting force.

choices.label: D
choices.text: a mixing of two different air masses.

explanation: Thunderstorm development requires three ingredients: conditionally unstable air, sufficient moisture (high humidity), and a lifting force (mechanism) to trigger and sustain the convection.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: An inversion tends to suppress, not promote, thunderstorm convection by capping vertical development.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Stratus cloud is a stable, layered cloud type, the opposite of the convective (cumuliform) cloud environment thunderstorms need.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Simple mixing of air masses does not by itself supply the needed instability and lifting force for a thunderstorm.

learning_objective: Describe the typical weather characteristics of an air mass being cooled from below.
question_text: Air masses that are being cooled from below are characterized by

choices.label: A
choices.text: strong winds, cumulus cloud, good visibility.

choices.label: B
choices.text: uniform temperature, good visibility.

choices.label: C
choices.text: continuous rain, freezing temperature.

choices.label: D
choices.text: fog, poor visibility and layer cloud.

explanation: Cooling from below stabilizes the air near the surface, favouring fog, poor visibility, and layer (stratiform) cloud rather than convective activity.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Strong winds and cumulus cloud are more typical of an unstable air mass being warmed/cooled from above, not one stabilized by surface cooling.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Good visibility is not typical; surface cooling favours fog/haze and reduced visibility.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Continuous rain and freezing temperatures are not the defining characteristic of surface-cooled air masses in general.

learning_objective: Describe what happens to warm air during the passage of a cold front.
question_text: During the passage of a cold front

choices.label: A
choices.text: warm air is compressed as cold air rides over it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: temperature rises owing to increased pressure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: fog will always form from the interaction of warm and cold air.

choices.label: D
choices.text: warm air is lifted as colder air pushes under it.

explanation: A cold front is the leading edge of an advancing cold air mass, which undercuts and forcibly lifts the warmer air ahead of it, often abruptly.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Cold air undercuts and lifts the warm air; it does not ride over it (that describes a warm front's overrunning pattern instead).
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: There is no general rule that temperature rises from increased pressure during a cold-front passage; temperature typically drops after passage.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Fog is not an inevitable ('always') result of frontal passage; it depends on specific moisture and temperature conditions.

question_text: The following sequence of clouds is observed at an airport: cirrus, altostratus, nimbostratus. The observer should expect

choices.label: A
choices.text: the passage of a cold front.

choices.label: B
choices.text: anticyclonic weather.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the passage of a warm front.

choices.label: D
choices.text: clearing skies and a decrease in temperature.

explanation: The progression from high cirrus, through thickening and lowering altostratus, to nimbostratus is the classic cloud sequence preceding the passage of a warm front.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Cold front passage is more typically preceded by cumuliform development and a more abrupt weather change, not this gradually thickening/lowering layered sequence.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Anticyclonic (high-pressure) weather is generally associated with clear or fair conditions, not a thickening, lowering cloud sequence.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This sequence indicates deteriorating weather (thickening, lowering cloud, approaching precipitation), not clearing skies.

learning_objective: State the altimeter-reading error from flying without adjustment from a low- to a high-pressure area.
question_text: Failure to adjust the altimeter when flying from an area of low pressure to an area of higher pressure will result in the altimeter indicating

choices.label: A
choices.text: too high.

choices.label: B
choices.text: too low.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the pressure altitude.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the true altitude.

explanation: If the altimeter subscale is left set to the lower pressure value while actual pressure increases, the altimeter under-reads relative to true altitude — it indicates too low, meaning the aircraft is actually higher than the altimeter shows (the safer direction, unlike the 'high to low, look out below' hazard case).

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The altimeter reads too low, not too high, in this direction of pressure change with an un-updated setting.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Pressure altitude specifically refers to height measured with the standard 29.92 in. Hg setting, which is a different (and unrelated) concept from this scenario's indicated-altitude error.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Leaving the setting un-updated means the altimeter does NOT read true altitude; it under-reads it.
